title: RAG, source evidence, and honest abstention
intro: Retrieval-augmented generation supplies relevant source material before an answer is generated. It does not automatically make the sources correct or the final answer faithful. Today you will separate retrieval from generation, inspect supporting evidence, and build a document assistant that can say when its evidence is insufficient.
objectives: Describe ingestion, retrieval, context construction, generation, and citation checking.
Keep source identity and access policy attached to retrieved information.
Evaluate supported answers and no-answer behavior separately.

concepts.title: The pipeline has several failure points
concepts.text: A RAG system ingests documents, divides or structures their content, retrieves useful pieces, constructs model context, and produces an answer. A wrong answer can originate in outdated data, a missing chunk, poor ranking, misleading context, or unsupported generation. Inspect these stages separately. Chunking is a tradeoff: tiny pieces can lose necessary context while oversized pieces can dilute relevance or exceed the budget. Preserve document IDs, source locations, and freshness information so retrieval can be investigated.

concepts.title: A citation must support the claim
concepts.text: A model can produce a citation-looking reference that is absent or irrelevant. Check that cited IDs belong to the supplied evidence and inspect whether the passage supports the actual claim. Sources themselves can be wrong, contradictory, or obsolete, so source selection and ownership matter. Authorization should filter which documents a trusted user can retrieve before those documents enter model context. A prompt asking the model to hide private information is not a substitute for that boundary.

concepts.title: Abstention is a product behavior
concepts.text: Define what happens when there is no useful evidence or the evidence conflicts. The answer can explain that the available documents do not establish the requested fact and offer a appropriate next step. Do not fill gaps with a confident invented answer merely to make the demo look smooth. Evaluate answerability, retrieval quality, and faithfulness as different criteria. A simple extractive baseline can help inspect sources before you add an optional language-model generator.

example.run: Run python grounded_answer.py. This is an extractive source-checking demonstration, not a language-model generator.
example.context: A selected evidence record supplies a supported answer. The missing record produces abstention rather than a fabricated policy.
example.output:
Standard shipping takes 3 to 5 business days.
Source: FAQ-01
The available documents do not answer this question.
example.walkthrough: The stable source ID travels with the text. The function returns an answer and citations as separate structured fields. Missing evidence produces a different result with no citation rather than an unrelated reference. This exact-match extractive demonstration isolates evidence handling; it is not semantic retrieval or generative RAG. Your project will add a documented retrieval method and an optional generator behind the same evidence-aware contract.

exercises.title: Locate the source of failure
exercises.task: Describe a wrong answer caused by missing retrieval and a different wrong answer caused by unsupported generation.
exercises.hint: Inspect the retrieved passages before changing a prompt.
exercises.check: The two failures have different targeted fixes.

exercises.title: Validate a citation
exercises.task: Try a citation ID that is absent from the supplied evidence and one whose passage does not support the claim.
exercises.hint: Existence and support are separate checks.
exercises.check: Neither citation is accepted as proof of the claim.

exercises.title: Write a no-answer policy
exercises.task: Define the message for missing, conflicting, and outdated evidence.
exercises.hint: Explain the limitation and a useful next step rather than inventing a result.
exercises.check: A new user can distinguish no evidence from a service error.

mistakes: Assuming retrieval makes documents true or makes generated answers faithful.
Accepting a citation solely because its format looks correct.
Retrieving private content and relying on a prompt to conceal it later.
fde: Customer document assistants depend on permissions, source ownership, and operational trust. An FDE makes evidence traceable and separates what the documents establish from what the system cannot currently answer.

project.title: Source-grounded FAQ assistant
project.brief: A team wants answers from a small fictional policy collection. Build a retrieval-and-answer pipeline that preserves source IDs, displays supporting passages, and handles unanswered questions. Use a clearly labelled extractive or fixture baseline first; optionally connect a real model generator without weakening permission or citation checks.
deliverables: A small source collection with IDs, locations, and freshness notes.
A retrieval method with inspectable ranked results.
An answer contract including citations and a no-answer state.
A labelled question set covering support, conflict, and missing evidence.

milestones.title: Prepare sources
steps: Record source ownership, identity, and which users can read each document.
Create answerable and unanswerable queries before evaluating output.
milestones.check: The evidence needed for each expected answer is known.

milestones.title: Connect retrieval and answers
steps: Retrieve only permitted evidence and preserve its IDs.
Generate or extract an answer under a clearly labelled mode.
milestones.check: A reviewer can inspect which passages influenced the result.

milestones.title: Test grounding
steps: Check citation existence and claim support.
Test missing, conflicting, and outdated evidence behavior.
milestones.check: The assistant does not turn unavailable evidence into confident claims.

acceptance: Retrieved evidence retains source IDs and inspectable passages.
Trusted document-access policy is applied before context construction.
Answer citations refer to supplied evidence and support their claims.
Missing evidence produces a clear abstention result.
Retrieval and answer-quality failures are recorded separately.
tests: Supported answer and relevant source passage
Clear no-answer result with no invented citation
Documented conflict policy rather than silent certainty
That source is absent from retrieval and model context
extensions: Add a real generator adapter and compare it with the extractive baseline.
Evaluate two chunking strategies on the same held-out queries.
review: At which pipeline stage did a observed failure begin?
How did you verify citation support rather than format alone?
What keeps a private source out of an unauthorized user's context?

title: Agents, bounded workflows, and observable tool use
intro: A tool-using agent observes a situation, selects an action, receives a result, and may continue toward a goal. That loop is useful only when its authority, resource limits, and stop conditions are explicit. Today you will compare a fixed workflow with an agent loop and build a bounded research assistant over a small approved knowledge collection.
objectives: Distinguish a fixed workflow from model-directed action selection.
Enforce step, time, and budget limits in application code.
Record observable actions and results without depending on hidden model reasoning.

concepts.title: Use the least complex useful workflow
concepts.text: A fixed workflow follows a predefined sequence. An agent chooses some actions dynamically based on observations and a goal. If the task has a predictable structure, a fixed pipeline may be easier to test, operate, and explain. Dynamic choice adds failure possibilities such as repeated searches, invalid tools, and premature conclusions. Decide whether that flexibility improves the actual customer outcome enough to justify its cost.

concepts.title: Constraints must exist outside the prompt
concepts.text: Limit steps, wall-clock time, allowed tools, and resource spending in application logic. The model should not be able to extend its own budget or approve a forbidden action. Provide clear outcomes for completed work, insufficient evidence, tool failure, and exhausted budget. Repeated failed attempts should not amplify an incident indefinitely. If a tool has side effects, authorization and idempotency are additional requirements beyond a loop counter.

concepts.title: Observable traces support investigation
concepts.text: Record the proposed tool, validated arguments, accepted or rejected action, tool result category, elapsed time, and final outcome. These application-visible events are useful evidence. Do not depend on access to a model's hidden chain of thought or publish sensitive prompts and documents indiscriminately. A safe trace should let an operator reconstruct what the system did and why the application accepted it, even when the model's internal processing is unavailable.

example.run: Run python bounded_workflow.py. The action list is scripted fixture data, not model-directed agent behavior.
example.context: An application-enforced step budget stops an unfinished scripted workflow.
example.code:
actions = ["search policy", "read evidence", "search again", "search again"]
max_steps = 3
completed = False
for step, action in enumerate(actions, start=1):
    if step > max_steps:
        print("Stopped: step budget exhausted")
        break
    print(f"Step {step}: {action}")
    if action == "finish":
        completed = True
        break
print("Completed:", completed)
example.output:
Step 1: search policy
Step 2: read evidence
Step 3: search again
Stopped: step budget exhausted
Completed: False
example.walkthrough: enumerate supplies an explicit step number. The budget check happens before executing the next action. A completion flag distinguishes a stopped loop from a successful task. The fixture deliberately never finishes, exposing the budget outcome. In a real agent, a model adapter could propose actions, but the same application checks must remain authoritative. Add timeouts and tool validation rather than assuming a step count covers every failure.

exercises.title: Compare workflow and agent
exercises.task: Describe a task that only needs a fixed lookup and one that might benefit from dynamic research.
exercises.hint: Identify what decisions must vary between inputs.
exercises.check: The extra flexibility has a specific user benefit.

exercises.title: Test each stop outcome
exercises.task: Add finish, invalid-action, and failed-tool fixtures.
exercises.hint: Do not label every stopped loop completed.
exercises.check: Success, failure, and budget exhaustion remain distinguishable.

exercises.title: Design a safe trace
exercises.task: List the event fields needed to investigate tool execution without copying private document text.
exercises.hint: Use IDs, categories, timings, and validated action names.
exercises.check: The trace explains actions without depending on hidden reasoning.

mistakes: Adding an agent when a simpler fixed workflow solves the task.
Asking the model to stop without enforcing a resource boundary in code.
Treating hidden chain-of-thought access as a required operational log.
fde: Customers need predictable authority and operations more than a dramatic agent demonstration. An FDE chooses the simplest effective flow, constrains its actions, and makes failures understandable to the people who will operate it.

project.title: A bounded policy-research assistant
project.brief: A team needs a short evidence-based summary from approved fictional policy documents. Build a workflow with search, read, and finish actions, then optionally replace scripted action selection with a model adapter. Enforce resource limits, permitted tools, and no-answer behavior in code. The first version is read-only and cannot send messages or modify business records.
deliverables: An allowed-tool contract and fixed or model-selected action interface.
Application-enforced step, timeout, and budget policies.
An inspectable trace of actions and result categories.
Fixtures for success, tool failure, invalid action, and budget exhaustion.

milestones.title: Choose the flow
steps: Write the goal and allowed observations/actions.
Compare a fixed workflow with the proposed dynamic version.
milestones.check: The design includes a reason for any dynamic decisions.

milestones.title: Enforce limits
steps: Validate each action and apply step/time/resource limits before execution.
Separate completed, abstained, failed, and exhausted outcomes.
milestones.check: No action can authorize more tools or extend its own budget.

milestones.title: Observe and evaluate
steps: Record safe action/result events.
Run each failure fixture and inspect the final outcome.
milestones.check: The workflow always stops with a clear result.

acceptance: Only the documented read-only tools can execute.
Application code enforces step, timeout, and resource policies.
Completion, abstention, failure, and budget exhaustion are distinct.
Observable traces identify actions and results without hidden reasoning.
Success and failure fixtures terminate within the documented limits.
tests: Budget exhaustion rather than endless work
Bounded failure and useful final status
extensions: Add a model-selection adapter and compare it with the fixed workflow.
Detect repeated identical actions and explain the recovery policy.
review: Which decisions benefit from an agent instead of a fixed flow?
What observable events explain a failed run?

title: Compose and share a usable document assistant
intro: A document assistant becomes a product when a new user can understand its scope, ask a useful question, inspect the evidence, and recover from failure. Today you will combine earlier components behind one interface and evaluate the whole workflow. The project can begin in a clearly labelled offline mode and add real generation only after its evidence boundaries work.
objectives: Compose retrieval, answer contracts, source display, and useful interface states.
Test the complete user workflow rather than only individual functions.
Publish a scoped demonstration with honest operating limits.

concepts.title: Composition needs shared contracts
concepts.text: The frontend, retrieval layer, and answer generator need compatible data shapes. Define question input, answer text, source records, and status categories before connecting them. Preserve distinctions such as no evidence, invalid request, and temporarily unavailable service. A boolean success field alone may hide the information the interface needs to guide recovery. Reuse earlier validated components instead of implementing each boundary differently inside a new UI.

concepts.title: First-use guidance is part of the product
concepts.text: Explain what collection the assistant uses and offer representative starting questions. Show a loading state when work is in progress, an answer with inspectable source passages, and a useful no-answer state. Keep model/fixture identity clear. An attractive empty chat box can leave a user unsure what to ask and what to trust. A source panel must connect evidence to the specific answer, not merely list every document in the collection.

concepts.title: A shared demo needs a data policy
concepts.text: Use fictional or intentionally public documents for a public demonstration. Browser code cannot safely contain a private model API credential. A real-provider integration belongs in a trusted local or hosted backend with explicit configuration. An offline extractive demonstration is useful for workflow testing but must not be sold as measured model performance. Inspect the deployed application in a clean context and record what a new user could actually complete.

example.run: Run python answer_contract.py. The response is a fixture for a frontend contract, not a model call.
example.context: A structured response preserves the answer, evidence, and mode so a UI can display them honestly.
example.code:
import json

response = {
    "status": "answered",
    "mode": "extractive-fixture",
    "answer": "Standard shipping takes 3 to 5 business days.",
    "sources": [{"id": "FAQ-01", "passage": "Standard shipping takes 3 to 5 business days."}],
}
print("Status:", response["status"])
print("Mode:", response["mode"])
print("Sources:", len(response["sources"]))
assert json.loads(json.dumps(response)) == response
example.walkthrough: The response separates status from answer text and preserves a source record with a stable ID. The mode tells the interface whether it is showing a fixture, extractive baseline, or real provider result. The JSON round trip checks that this sample can cross a frontend/backend boundary. It does not prove answer correctness or a working deployment. Test those separately through representative questions and actual user interaction.

exercises.title: Design interface states
exercises.task: Sketch ready, loading, answered, no-evidence, and failed states.
exercises.hint: Each state should tell the user what happened and what they can do next.
exercises.check: A service error is not presented as an unsupported factual answer.

exercises.title: Trace one question
exercises.task: Follow a question through input validation, retrieval, answer creation, and source display.
exercises.hint: Check the contract at each boundary.
exercises.check: The visible source actually supports the displayed answer.

exercises.title: Observe a stranger test
exercises.task: Ask a new user to answer a policy question using only your interface.
exercises.hint: Record any coaching you had to provide.
exercises.check: You have a concrete usability finding and a retested improvement.

mistakes: Combining components without agreeing on their input/output shapes.
Showing every source instead of evidence relevant to the answer.
Publishing private documents or putting provider credentials in browser code.
fde: An FDE turns working components into a customer workflow with a useful handoff. Integration, onboarding, evidence display, and deployment verification are all part of the result the customer can use.

project.title: A shareable document-assistant demo
project.brief: Create a usable interface for the grounded assistant from lesson 19. Include example questions, answer/source display, no-evidence and failure states, and an honest mode label. Publish a fictional-data demo or document a reproducible local version while a trusted backend is being prepared. A real-provider extension must keep credentials out of the frontend.
deliverables: A usable interface connected to the validated answer contract.
A fictional/public document collection and scope explanation.
A verified demo URL or a reproducible local delivery record.
A workflow test report and one observed usability improvement.

milestones.title: Connect contracts
steps: Agree on question, answer, source, status, and mode fields.
Reuse the existing retrieval and evidence checks.
milestones.check: The interface receives enough information to display the correct state.

milestones.title: Build the whole task
steps: Add starting questions, loading feedback, and inspectable sources.
Handle absent evidence and service errors differently.
milestones.check: A new user can tell what the assistant knows and how to inspect it.

milestones.title: Verify and share
steps: Test a clean context using only fictional/public data.
Observe a new user and record the actual delivery mode and limits.
milestones.check: The demonstration's scope and verification evidence are clear.

acceptance: The interface states its document scope and actual execution mode.
Answered results display relevant supporting passages.
No-evidence and service-failure states are distinguishable and useful.
The demo contains no private documents or browser-exposed credentials.
A new-user workflow and delivery verification are recorded.
tests: Supported answer and relevant source display
Recovery-oriented service error, not invented success
Clean browser or fresh local setup
extensions: Connect a trusted provider backend after lesson 24.
Collect explicitly scoped feedback without storing unnecessary personal data.
review: What could a new user do without your coaching?
How does the interface distinguish scope limits from service failure?
Which part of the delivery still needs verification?

title: Evaluation datasets, rubrics, and regression analysis
intro: Evaluation makes a quality claim inspectable. A fixed set of inputs and a clear rubric help you compare revisions, but the dataset's coverage and the scoring method still matter. Today you will build a repeatable evaluation harness for your document assistant and report different failure categories rather than hiding them inside one impressive score.
objectives: Create labelled evaluation cases with observable acceptance criteria.
Separate retrieval, answer support, abstention, and operational failure metrics.
Compare revisions while recording dataset identity and scoring limits.

concepts.title: A dataset represents a chosen workload
concepts.text: Choose examples from the tasks and failure modes your intended users face. Include common questions, ambiguous questions, missing evidence, adversarial text, and permission boundaries. Keep stable case IDs and a dataset version so results can be compared. A tiny curated dataset is useful for regression checks, but it is limited evidence about broad future traffic. Record which cases were used to tune the system and which were held out.

concepts.title: A rubric defines observable quality
concepts.text: For document answers, consider whether relevant evidence was retrieved, claims are supported, the answer addresses the question, and abstention is appropriate. Operational checks such as timeouts and permissions are separate from fluent wording. A model judge can help scale scoring, but it has its own errors and needs calibration against human judgments. Define what a pass means and preserve the actual outputs that led to the score.

concepts.title: Comparisons need controlled context
concepts.text: Record source versions, prompt version, model/configuration, retrieval settings, and scoring method. Otherwise a score change may come from a changed dataset or source collection rather than the implementation revision you intended to test. Inspect regressions by case and category. An average improvement can conceal a failure on the specific workflow the customer most needs. Re-run critical cases after changing any pipeline boundary.

example.run: Run python eval_report.py. Results are illustrative scored fixtures, not measured live-model results.
example.context: Two categories are reported separately so an abstention failure does not disappear inside an overall average.
example.code:
cases = [
    {"id": "Q1", "category": "supported", "passed": True},
    {"id": "Q2", "category": "supported", "passed": True},
    {"id": "Q3", "category": "abstention", "passed": False},
]
for category in sorted({case["category"] for case in cases}):
    group = [case for case in cases if case["category"] == category]
    passed = sum(case["passed"] for case in group)
    print(f"{category}: {passed}/{len(group)}")
print("Failed IDs:", ', '.join(case["id"] for case in cases if not case["passed"]))
example.walkthrough: Stable case IDs connect the summary to individual evidence. The category set defines the groups, and each group receives a numerator and denominator. Sorting makes the demonstration output deterministic. Reporting the failed ID keeps the underlying defect visible. The fixture does not run a model or justify a quality claim; your project harness will obtain outputs from a clearly named system mode and apply a reviewed rubric.

exercises.title: Write a rubric
exercises.task: Define supported, unsupported, and partially supported answer criteria using concrete examples.
exercises.hint: Do not make confidence or word count the correctness criterion.
exercises.check: Two reviewers can discuss disagreements using the same criteria.

exercises.title: Find a hidden regression
exercises.task: Create two result versions where overall score improves but a critical category worsens.
exercises.hint: Inspect counts and case IDs, not only a rounded percentage.
exercises.check: Your report makes the critical regression visible.

exercises.title: Preserve reproducibility
exercises.task: Record source, prompt, model/mode, dataset, and scoring versions for one run.
exercises.hint: A filename alone may not identify what data was used.
exercises.check: A reviewer can reproduce the intended comparison conditions.

mistakes: Reporting one overall score without category coverage or denominators.
Tuning on every evaluation case and then claiming independent validation.
Treating an uncalibrated model judge as an unquestionable ground truth.
fde: A customer's success criteria should become checks the team can repeat. An FDE connects the metric to the real workload and explains both observed improvement and remaining failure categories.

project.title: A repeatable document-assistant evaluation harness
project.brief: Build a harness for at least 20 labelled questions or boundary cases. Run the grounded assistant under a named execution mode, save its actual outputs, score them using a documented rubric, and compare two versions. Include supported answers, no-evidence behavior, permission checks, and failures. Report critical regressions even if an overall average improves.
deliverables: A versioned dataset with at least 20 stable case IDs.
A rubric and repeatable run/scoring command.
Per-case output records and category summaries.
A before/after report identifying regressions and limits.

milestones.title: Design coverage
steps: Choose categories from real or fictional user workflows.
Write expected evidence or behavior before generating answers.
milestones.check: The dataset includes more than easy happy-path questions.

milestones.title: Build the harness
steps: Run a named mode and save actual case results.
Apply the rubric consistently and preserve human-review notes.
milestones.check: An operator can rerun the suite without manually reconstructing it.

milestones.title: Compare revisions
steps: Hold comparison inputs constant and record changed system settings.
Inspect critical failures by ID and category.
milestones.check: The report can justify a change or explain why it should not ship.

acceptance: At least 20 labelled cases have stable IDs and documented coverage.
The harness has a repeatable run command and a reviewed rubric.
Actual outputs and execution mode are recorded per case.
Summaries show category counts, denominators, and failed IDs.
A two-version comparison reports regressions and verification limits.
tests: Rubric assesses retrieval and claim support separately
Access boundary is checked as a critical requirement
Improved average but worsened critical category
Report exposes the regression rather than hiding it
extensions: Calibrate automated judge scores against a reviewed human sample.
Add latency and cost reporting with explicit measurement scope.
review: What user workload does the dataset represent?
Which critical failure would block a release despite a higher average score?

title: Permissions, prompt injection, budgets, and operating cost
intro: Production AI is a surrounding system of data boundaries, application permissions, resource limits, and recovery behavior. A model prompt cannot enforce all of those responsibilities. Today you will threat-model a narrow document-assistant workflow and implement permission and budget gates outside generation.
objectives: Distinguish untrusted instruction-like content from trusted application authority.
Apply document permissions and resource limits before work is executed.
Estimate operating cost and test abuse/failure cases under an explicit scope.

concepts.title: Untrusted content can contain instructions
concepts.text: A user message or retrieved document can ask the assistant to ignore rules, disclose data, or perform an unauthorized action. Treat that text as data within your defined task, not a trusted change to application policy. Delimiters and prompt wording can help model behavior, but permission checks must remain in code and the data layer. Minimize what the model can access so a model failure does not automatically expose everything in the customer environment.

concepts.title: Enforce authority and resource budgets
concepts.text: Use trusted user identity to decide which documents and tools can be used. Check limits before an expensive operation and define what happens when the limit is reached. Rate limits, per-request token budgets, timeouts, and step counts address different resource dimensions. If multiple workers share a spending or request limit, a naive in-memory counter is not a complete production enforcement mechanism. Document the scope of your lesson prototype rather than claiming it protects distributed traffic.

concepts.title: Cost estimates need operational assumptions
concepts.text: State traffic volume, usage per task, provider prices, retrieval/index cost, and hosting assumptions. Distinguish estimated demand from measured demand. Include unexpected retries and large inputs in the analysis. Useful alerts need an owner and a response, not merely a dashboard number. Security tests against five sample attacks provide limited evidence about those cases; they do not prove that every future injection or data-leak path is impossible.

example.run: Run python policy_gate.py. This is a single-process authorization fixture, not a complete identity system.
example.context: The trusted caller supplies identity separately from the question or model output.
example.output:
public-faq allowed
internal-pricing forbidden
Model text cannot change the trusted permission map
example.walkthrough: The policy maps trusted fixture identities to permitted resource IDs. The default set denies unknown users rather than granting broad access. The gate is applied before selecting a document for context. A real service must authenticate the caller; accepting a user_id supplied freely in a browser request would not establish trusted identity. The model cannot override this map merely by returning an admin role in its output.

exercises.title: Draw trust boundaries
exercises.task: Mark user input, retrieved text, trusted identity, policy, and tool execution on your pipeline diagram.
exercises.hint: Do not place trusted authority inside model-provided text.
exercises.check: You can name the enforcement point for each protected resource.

exercises.title: Budget a failure
exercises.task: Estimate cost with normal traffic, doubled output length, and repeated retry attempts using fictional prices.
exercises.hint: Show assumptions and separate each cost component.
exercises.check: The reader can reproduce the arithmetic and see its limits.

exercises.title: Attack a scoped fixture
exercises.task: Test instruction-like document text asking to reveal a forbidden source.
exercises.hint: Inspect what reaches retrieval and context, not just the final wording.
exercises.check: The forbidden source remains absent regardless of the text's request.

mistakes: Using a model-generated role or a user-supplied ID as trusted authority.
Relying on a prompt to protect data that was already retrieved.
Calling a small attack sample or single-process counter a complete production defense.
fde: Customers have permission rules, cost constraints, and operators who need to recover from failures. An FDE translates those constraints into enforceable boundaries and explicitly scopes the claims supported by the tests.

project.title: A permission and budget boundary for the assistant
project.brief: Harden the fictional document assistant with trusted-user fixtures, document filtering, request limits, and explicit exhausted-budget behavior. Add a small threat model and abuse test set. Keep the prototype's limits visible: fixture identity and single-process budgets demonstrate boundaries but are not a deployed authentication or distributed-quota system.
deliverables: A trust-boundary diagram and protected-resource list.
Permission filtering before context construction.
Explicit request/resource limits and recovery results.
An abuse-test report and a reproducible cost estimate.

milestones.title: Define the policy
steps: Specify which trusted users may access each source and tool.
List untrusted inputs and likely misuse paths.
milestones.check: Protected data is identified before implementation.

milestones.title: Enforce before execution
steps: Filter forbidden documents before retrieval/context use.
Apply scoped resource gates before expensive work.
milestones.check: A rejected request cannot consume the same unrestricted workflow as an accepted one.

milestones.title: Test and estimate
steps: Run malicious-text, unknown-user, and budget-exhaustion cases.
Document cost assumptions, alert ownership, and prototype limitations.
milestones.check: The report distinguishes observed defenses from untested attack space.

acceptance: Trusted authority is separate from user text and model arguments.
Forbidden documents never enter an unauthorized user's context.
Resource limits are enforced outside the model prompt.
Budget exhaustion and policy rejection produce clear outcomes.
The threat model, attack results, and cost assumptions are recorded.
tests: Retrieved text requests an admin override
Policy map and allowed resources remain unchanged
Unknown identity or exhausted resource budget
extensions: Replace fixture identity with a verified authentication boundary in a later backend iteration.
Design shared quota storage and concurrency checks for multi-worker operation.
review: Which check enforces authority outside model output?
What happens before and after the budget gate?
What would be misleading about calling the prototype fully secure?

title: Backend APIs, databases, and durable feedback
intro: A backend owns shared rules and durable state behind a contract other programs can use. Today you will connect HTTP input validation, database operations, and explicit error behavior. Your project is a small FastAPI feedback service for the assistant, with parameterized SQL and a documented trust boundary.
objectives: Specify API methods, request fields, response fields, and failure categories.
Store and retrieve records using parameterized SQL.
Distinguish request validation, authentication, authorization, and database consistency.

concepts.title: An API is a caller-facing contract
concepts.text: Describe what POST /feedback accepts, what a successful response contains, and which invalid inputs are rejected. HTTP validation and domain validation are related but different: a string can be structurally valid while being an empty or unauthorized source reference. FastAPI can parse and validate declared request shapes, but your application still owns domain rules and resource permissions. Keep responses stable enough for callers to handle them deliberately.

concepts.title: SQL separates values from commands
concepts.text: Parameterized queries pass values separately from SQL text. Building SQL by joining arbitrary input into a command risks confusing data with executable syntax. Use stable record IDs and constraints appropriate to the model. Transactions group related changes that must succeed or fail together. A single-process SQLite demonstration helps teach durable data, but production concurrency, migrations, backups, and recovery need their own operating plan.

concepts.title: Trusted identity and validation are different
concepts.text: A valid feedback payload does not establish who sent it or whether they may inspect another user's feedback. Authenticate at a trusted boundary, then authorize the requested operation. For a local lesson prototype, a clearly labelled identity fixture can demonstrate policy, but a free-form user ID header is not production authentication. Keep provider credentials on the backend and avoid returning private internals in error responses.

example.run: Run python feedback_store.py. It uses an in-memory SQLite database to demonstrate the storage operation; the project adds file persistence and HTTP endpoints.
example.context: User content is a parameter value, not part of the SQL command structure.
example.code:
import sqlite3

connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.execute("CREATE TABLE feedback (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, note TEXT NOT NULL)")
note = "The source passage helped me check the answer."
with connection:
    connection.execute("INSERT INTO feedback (note) VALUES (?)", (note,))
row = connection.execute("SELECT id, note FROM feedback WHERE id = ?", (1,)).fetchone()
print("Stored feedback:", row[0])
print(row[1])
connection.close()
example.output:
Stored feedback: 1
The source passage helped me check the answer.
example.walkthrough: The connection creates a temporary in-memory database. The placeholder question mark marks a value position, and the tuple supplies the value separately. The connection context manages transaction success or failure, and the later explicit close releases the connection. The SELECT also uses a parameter. An in-memory database disappears when closed, so a durable service must use a documented file path or another persistence system and test a real restart.

exercises.title: Write the endpoint contract
exercises.task: Specify feedback input, successful output, invalid input, and missing-record behavior before implementing HTTP handlers.
exercises.hint: Use concrete example requests and responses.
exercises.check: A frontend developer can build against the contract without reading database internals.

exercises.title: Separate data from SQL
exercises.task: Store a note containing quotation marks through a parameterized query.
exercises.hint: Pass it as a value instead of escaping it into command text.
exercises.check: The complete note is stored as data and the table still exists.

exercises.title: Test durable restart
exercises.task: Change the demonstration to a disposable file database and inspect it after reopening the connection.
exercises.hint: Document the file location and commit behavior.
exercises.check: The record remains after process restart.

mistakes: Concatenating request input into SQL commands.
Treating a valid request schema as authentication or authorization.
Claiming persistence based only on an in-memory database demonstration.
fde: An FDE connects customer-facing workflows to trusted shared state. The API contract, permission boundary, and database operating story should be understandable to both the integration team and the future operator.

project.title: FastAPI feedback and question service
project.brief: Build POST /feedback, GET /feedback/{id}, and POST /ask for the fictional assistant. Use validated request models, a documented SQLite file, parameterized queries, and a trusted-identity boundary or explicitly labelled local identity fixtures. Reuse your answer contract and make invalid, missing, and forbidden outcomes clear. Verify the current FastAPI installation command in the linked documentation.
deliverables: An API contract and runnable FastAPI service with documented setup.
A durable feedback schema and parameterized storage layer.
Request validation and explicitly scoped access checks.
HTTP, restart, and invalid-input test results.

milestones.title: Agree on the API
steps: Write request/response examples for the three endpoints.
Define domain rules and the identity/permission scope.
milestones.check: Invalid and forbidden cases have different documented outcomes.

milestones.title: Connect durable storage
steps: Implement parameterized writes and reads against a file database.
Keep SQL and provider configuration out of frontend code.
milestones.check: A restart preserves feedback and a quote-containing note remains intact.

milestones.title: Test the integration
steps: Exercise real HTTP handlers with success and failure cases.
Document startup, data location, backup, and prototype identity limits.
milestones.check: The service can be reproduced and its security claims match the implemented boundary.

acceptance: The three endpoints follow documented request/response contracts.
Invalid payloads and domain-rule failures are rejected clearly.
Feedback survives a process restart in the documented database.
Database values use parameterized SQL rather than command concatenation.
Trusted identity or fixture limits and access checks are explicitly tested.
tests: Valid feedback then lookup by ID
Stored record returned under the documented contract
Validation failure without a stored invalid record
Note containing quotes or SQL-looking text
Stored as data; schema remains intact
Persistence verified and unauthorized access rejected
extensions: Add a versioned schema migration and test upgrade from a sample older database.
Introduce verified authentication and multi-user tests before claiming production account isolation.
review: Which rules belong to schema validation versus authorization?
What makes the SQL operation safe for arbitrary note text?
What evidence proves the feedback is actually durable?
